many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC task pattern notes

## Diagonal marker(s) encode a periodic color tiling (task-adfd3b86)
For this task family, infer a periodic 2D color pattern from the colored diagonals, then tile it across the entire original grid, replacing background cells. Demos establish a small-period pattern, often with a diagonal-period structure; do not merely preserve the sparse diagonal input.

Accepted test: 18x18 input had background 0 and two down-right diagonals: color 5 at (1-based) (r6,c1) through (r18,c13), and color 6 at (r11,c1) through (r18,c8). Correct output was an 18x18 checkerboard alternating 6 and 5: row 1 begins `6 5 6 5 ...` and each next row shifts one cell, so output[r,c] = 6 when (r+c) is even (1-based), else 5. Accepted with 0 wrong submissions after six demonstration requests.

Useful demos and interpretation:
- Demo 6 (6x6): input had anti-diagonal color 2 plus terminal 6/9 markers; output was a 3-color checker-like period-3 pattern `6 9 2` repeated across rows, shifting left by one each row. This indicates the diagonal marker motif encodes a periodic tiling, and the output may be an alternating/diagonal periodic field over the whole grid.
- Demo 5 (19x19): sparse diagonal motifs with colors 1, 7, 9 yielded a period-4 tiled output using sequence 1,9,7,1 repeated along rows, with each row shifted left by one; equivalently period in r+c (verify phase from the demo). Demo 3 similarly yielded a five-step diagonal-periodic tiling with colors 5,2,6,7,5 in sequence (period 4 distinct colors; 5 repeated at cycle seam). In that demo, color seed loci at diagonal offsets -21,-20,-19,-18 and +4 fit a period-4 color assignment on the diagonal coordinate; output rows shift the same sequence by one per row. Demo 6's anti-diagonal seeds analogously produced period-3 tiling. Other demonstrations include 1D full-width color stripes with periodic repetitions, so identify the motif's repeating sequence and phase from the actual demo.

Practical approach: inspect nonzero/colored loci and determine the underlying diagonal or row/column repeat period and phase; produce the complete output grid with the corresponding periodic colors. The test solved here reduced to a 2-color checkerboard, not a plain single-color fill or preservation of the input markers. Do not overcomplicate with unsupported modulo arithmetic; directly verify candidate rule against demo output rows/cells before submitting. Other instances in this family can encode longer periods: infer the actual modulo and color phase from multiple marker diagonals, rather than assuming every input becomes a checkerboard. Further accepted instance (27x27): parallel down-right diagonals had color 5 at d=c-r=6, color 1 at d=16, and color 1 at d=-7. The accepted output was a period-3 diagonal tiling: output 5 iff (c-r) mod 3 = 0, otherwise 1. The seed offsets satisfy this: 6 ≡ 0, 16 ≡ 1, and -7 ≡ 2 (mod 3), with latter two both 1. This solved after the first guess (a 23-period band fill) was incorrect. Infer the smallest modulo matching all seed-line colors, then extend its color mapping to every residue; here the observed residues 1 and 2 share color 1, residue 0 is 5. Output colors across full grid, not just marker lines.

## Sparse-marker line fill (observed in task-096cc299)

Demos show a uniform background (demo: 2, markers: 1; another: 1/7; test: 9/0) with a third color (demo output: 3). Preserve all original marker cells and background cells not changed by the rule. For each row, sort the marker positions and fill every background cell strictly between each consecutive pair of markers with 3. Do the same independently for each column: sort marker rows and fill every background cell strictly between consecutive markers in that column with 3. The fill is only axis-aligned; do not extrapolate beyond the first/last marker, and don't fill diagonal spaces. Markers remain their original color. Equivalently: for every pair of consecutive same-marker cells in any row or column, color the gap with 3. In overlaps, still 3.

## Horizontal right-tail recoloring (observed task-705b0a10)

Across the demonstrations, recolor to 1 the right-side tail of the unique horizontal pattern row, keeping all other cells and rows unchanged. The tail begins immediately after the pattern's rightmost non-background component and runs through the grid's right edge. Examples: demo1 changed rows 4–5, columns 9–10 from 6 to 1 after a pattern reaching column 8; demo2 changed rows 4–7, columns 18–22 from 4 to 1 after a pattern reaching column 17; demo3 changed only row 8, columns 9–14 from 2 to 1 after the 0/2 pattern reached column 8 (row 13's zeros continued and were not changed); demo4 changed row 7, columns 9–21 from 9 to 1 after 7s through column 8. Test input had 8s through column 13 on row 1, with a lone 5 at column 14; recoloring that single trailing cell to 1 was accepted. Do not color unrelated uniform rows.

Practical implementation: copy input; scan each row and each column; identify positions with the non-background marker; for each adjacent pair in the sorted positions, set cells strictly between them to 3. Preserve all other cells. Check the dimensions and transcribe carefully—my first incorrect submission omitted a few correct vertical/horizontal gap cells, while the final answer using the rule was accepted.

### Evidence
- Demo 2 (25x9): background 2, marker 1, output fills between consecutive markers horizontally and vertically with 3; e.g. column 5 becomes 3 in gaps between marker rows; bottom row fills the gap between two 1 markers.
- Demo 3 (9x30): background 1, marker 7, output fills marker gaps along rows/columns with 3; gaps stop at endpoints and outside markers remain background.
- Test (27x18): background 9, marker 0; final submission applying the rule was accepted.
- Additional test (26x19): background 0, marker 8; applying the same rule, with fill color 3, was accepted. The grid had many isolated markers and some runs; fill only between consecutive 8s in each row and column. The rule is consistent across different background and marker colors.
- Additional test (12x30): background 2, marker 0; only two markers appeared in row 1 at columns 11 and 29 (1-based), so fill columns 12–28 with 3. Other isolated markers remain unchanged. Submission was accepted, reaffirming that fills are only made between consecutive markers on the same row or column.
- Additional test (task-096cc299, 10x19): background 7, marker 2, fill 3. The accepted output was computed by independently filling gaps between consecutive 2s in each row and column, preserving all endpoints and all other cells. This recurrence had 0 wrong submissions. Sparse/isolated markers leave no fill; gaps may be length 1 or many cells, and orthogonal row/column fills can overlap without changing the result.

- Additional accepted recurrence instance (task-705b0a10, 22x16): a repeated 2-row motif appears at the top and again near the bottom, with background 0 and motif color 5. The lower copy has a right-tail region on both rows after the motif's rightmost component; recolor that tail (columns 12–16, 1-based) from 0 to 1, preserving the motif and all other cells. Accepted with 0 wrong submissions. This supports the existing horizontal right-tail rule even when the target pattern is duplicated vertically: only the lower/right-side tail clearly designated by the copy's extension is changed.
- Additional accepted recurrence instance (task-096cc299, 10x25): background 0, marker 6, fill color 3. Independently fill only cells strictly between consecutive 6s in each row and column; preserve endpoints and all other 0s. Correct on the first submission. This confirms the same rule for a 10x25 grid and this color combination.
- Additional accepted recurrence instance (task-096cc299, 10x20): background 9, marker 1, fill 3. The test contained horizontal gaps (row 4 between columns 8 and 16; row 9 between columns 13 and 19) and vertical gaps (including consecutive marker pairs in columns 4, 5, 10, 12, and 18). Filling every strictly-between cell for consecutive same-row/same-column marker pairs and preserving all other cells was accepted with 0 wrong submissions. Adjacent markers require no intervening fill.
- Additional accepted recurrence instance (task-096cc299, 22x18): background 1, marker 0, fill 3. Independently fill gaps between consecutive 0s in each row and each column, preserving marker 0s and all untouched 1s; accepted on the first submission (0 wrong attempts). Compute by copying the input and scanning rows and columns for markers in the original grid so newly filled 3s do not affect detection. Confirms the rule on a 22x18 input with dense background and adjacent marker runs.

- Additional accepted recurrence instance (task-705b0a10, 11x10): background 8, motif color 9. The distinctive two-row horizontal pattern occupies rows 3–4 (1-based). Recolor its right-side background tail, columns 8–10, to 1 in both pattern rows; leave the internal background gap and all other rows/cells unchanged. Accepted on the first submission (0 wrong attempts). This confirms that the endpoint is the rightmost motif-colored cell in each relevant pattern row, and the tail runs from the following column to the right edge; modify only the motif rows, not the visually uniform rows or separate lower 9-pattern rows.
- Additional accepted recurrence instance (task-705b0a10, 24x15): background 2, motif 7. Two matching horizontal pattern copies occur at rows 3–4 and 14–15 (1-based). In the lower copy, recolor only row 15's background tail (columns 12–15) to 1, immediately after the rightmost 7 at column 11. Do not also recolor row 14, which has a gap at column 11 then background to the edge; despite being part of the motif pair, that row is not the designated tail. First attempt coloring both lower rows was wrong; second, row 14 alone, was wrong; accepted with only row 15 c12–15 changed. This clarifies that when repeated motif copies exist, identify the specifically designated copy/row and recolor only the contiguous motif run's trailing background, not a whole pair. Demo corroboration: in another example, a lower row with 7s through c18 and background c19–25 changed to 1 across c19–25, while an isolated full-width 7 row remained unchanged. Preserve all unrelated cells.
- Accepted recurrence instance (task-705b0a10, 29x9): background 0, bar color 4; full-width row 3 is unchanged, but two shorter bars lower in the grid are both extended by recoloring their right-side tails to 1. Row 16 has 4s in columns 1–5, so change c6–9 to 1; row 24 has 4s in c1–4, so change c5–9 to 1. Both edits are required: attempts that changed only one of the two partial rows were incorrect; changing both was accepted. Preserve the full-width row and every unrelated cell. This is evidence that a test can contain multiple qualifying partial horizontal bars, and all designated right tails need recoloring.
- Further accepted recurrence instance (task-705b0a10, 27x12): background 6, motif color 8, tail color 1. A repeated pattern appears in an upper and lower region. In the lower copy, recolor only the right-side background tails of the two partial 8-rows: row 22 columns 8–12 and row 24 columns 8–12 (1-based). Leave the upper copy, intervening motif rows, and all other cells unchanged. Accepted on the first submission. This supports changing all designated partial horizontal bar tails in the selected lower copy while preserving full-width rows.
- Additional accepted recurrence instance (task-705b0a10, 28x22): background 9, motif 4, tail color 1. The repeated 4-pattern occurs in an upper block (rows 7–10) and a lower block (rows 22–25). Only the lower block's rows 22 and 24 have designated right-edge tail cells: change row 22 column 22 and row 24 column 22 from 9 to 1; preserve rows 23 and 25 and the upper pattern entirely. Accepted after one incorrect attempt. The incorrect attempt changed column 22 on all four lower rows, so do not recolor every row merely because it belongs to a repeated block; identify the specific designated partial horizontal bars/tail rows. A demo for this recurrence also changed just one cell within a pattern row's right-end sequence, reinforcing that modifications can be single-cell tails.
- New accepted instance (task-705b0a10, 29x11): background 9, motif 8. Input row 1 was `9 9 8 9 9 9 9 9 9 9 9`; the accepted output changed row 1 columns 4–11 to 1, keeping the 8 at c3 and all other cells unchanged. A large lower motif at row 13 (`c3–c11` all 8) and rows 14–15 (`c1–c2` 8s) remained unchanged. So do not automatically edit only the lowest repeated block: identify the designated short motif/run with a background tail to its right; in this instance the isolated top-row 8 marked the start of a tail that became 1 through the right edge. This exact instance was solved after an initial unchanged-grid submission was wrong. A matching demo showed only the bottom-most short 5-run row recolored through the right edge, while other repeated motifs stayed intact, supporting selective tail recoloring rather than changing every structural copy.

## Unsolved split-grid task (task-f0199aba; preserve uncertainty)

Input has a random-looking 9-row field above a full-width color-4 separator, then a 9-row field below it. One demo used 21 columns: upper field colors 1/5, lower field colors 2/5; output is 9x21, almost entirely 5 with sparse 3s. Test uses upper colors 2/6, lower 2/5, separator 4, and is 21x15. This instance was not solved despite 8 submissions; none of attempted outputs are reliable. The hypothesis that output is simply top-marker locations recolored to 3 (or intersections with a vertically flipped/rotated lower half) was repeatedly wrong. Do not reuse that guess; inspect any recurrence carefully and request demos if necessary. Demo output 3 coordinates (1-based rows/cols): r1 c3; r2 c21; r3 c13,c15; r4 c10; r5 c8,c14,c15,c20; r6 c4,c6,c8; r7 c3,c13,c19; r8 c11,c18,c21; r9 c12,c15. All other output cells are 5. Upper demo field has 5 markers amid 1; lower is 2/5. There may be a nontrivial spatial/color correspondence. One attempt was also invalid due to submitting 14 rather than 21 columns. Treat rule as unknown.

## task-f0199aba: horizontal separator / 2-column test (failed; rule unresolved)

This recurrence needs careful handling; do not apply the known vertical-separator rule without verifying geometry and color logic. Current failed instance input had 29 rows × 2 columns, with row 15 `0 0` as a horizontal separator. Rows 1–14 are the upper field; rows 16–29 are lower field, so there are two 14×2 fields. Upper values are 8/1, lower values 4/1. Eight submissions all failed. Their outputs were mostly 14×2 grids using 9 as assumed base and 3 in guessed match/marker locations; no accepted feedback beyond incorrect, so none of these guesses is supported.

One requested demonstration was 15×10 with a full-width row 8 of color 6 separating two 7×10 fields. Upper field background 9, with 8 markers at (r5,c3) and (r6,c7); lower field background 9, with 0 markers at (r2,c3) and (r7,c2), using field-relative 1-based rows. Output was 7×10, all 3 except 9 at (r1,c3), (r5,c3), (r6,c7), and (r7,c2). Thus the output marks 3 almost everywhere and leaves 9 at the union of marker positions in either half; the separator is removed. This differs from prior hypotheses about matching corresponding cells and base-color output. For a recurrence with this structure, test the union-complement pattern: initialize output to 3, then place the common background color at locations where either corresponding half contains a non-background marker. However, treat this as tentative until confirming the exact encoding; the failed 29×2 instance does not straightforwardly establish its own output colors/base (marker sets are nonuniform and include 1s as backgrounds/markers ambiguously). Request another demo if budget allows rather than repeat the unsuccessful guesses.

Important process lesson: count the separator and split fields precisely, then derive output from the demo cell-by-cell before submitting. The demo separator was row 8 (not a vertical divider). Do not use the unrelated vertical-divider equality rule below for horizontal-separator instances.

## Solved split-grid task (task-f0199aba; new evidence)
A later instance clarified and solved the vertical-separator variant. The input has two equal-sized fields separated by a full-height vertical separator column. Compare the two fields cell-by-cell in corresponding row/column positions. Output has the field dimensions, uses the dominant/background color of the left field as its base, and places color 3 exactly where the two input field cell values are equal. All other output cells are the left-field background color. This rule solved a 9x23 instance (two 9x11 fields) with 0 incorrect submissions. Do not assume this rule applies to the horizontal-separator variant above.

Evidence:
- Demo 5x15: fields are each 5x7, separator is column 8 (color 9). Left field background 1 with sparse 4s; right field uses 8/1. Output is 5x7, background 1, with 3s exactly where both corresponding cells equal 1: (1,3), (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (5,2). For instance, (5,6) is not marked because left=4 and right=8.
- Solved test 9x23: fields are each 9x11, separator is column 12 (color 5). Left field background 6 with sparse 4s; right field is mostly 1 with two 6s. Output is 9x11, background 6; the only matching cell value at corresponding positions was row 5, column 5 (both fields have 6), so that cell is 3. The other right-side 6 at row 3, column 3 aligns with left value 4 and is not marked. Accepted, 0 wrong attempts.

Implementation: split around separator; retain only the left field's background color as output base, then for each corresponding coordinate set output to 3 if left_value == right_value. Keep output dimensions equal to either field. This replaces the earlier unresolved status for the task; do not use prior speculative marker/intersection guesses.

### Further recurrence evidence (vertical separator; 2×19 test solved)
For a vertical separator, split the grid into equal-width fields and compare corresponding cells. In the confirmed examples, color 3 marks exact cell-value equality. The background/base output color is the unique color shared by the palettes of both fields (rather than necessarily the left field's most frequent color); when no positions match, output is uniformly that shared color. Evidence: demo 1 had left palette {0,6}, right palette {2,6}; output was all 6, consistent with no equal-position pairs and shared color 6. Demo 2 had left palette {1,2}, right palette {2,4}; output base was 2, with 3 exactly at corresponding equal-value positions. A test with two rows and separator column 10 had left palette {6,7}, right palette {4,6}; output was 2×9 of base 6, with a single 3 at row 2, column 4, the only matching pair. Accepted after two incorrect submissions (first wrong guess placed 3s at mismatched/assumed positions; second all-6 omitted the one equality).

Implementation: discard the separator column, set output dimensions to the field dimensions, find the sole color in the intersection of both field palettes for the base, then scan aligned cells and set output to 3 iff the two values are equal; otherwise leave the shared-color base. The example with no equal aligned values confirms base remains unchanged everywhere. Prior wording that the base is always the left-field dominant/background color is too narrow; use the shared palette color when the field backgrounds differ.

### Solved horizontal-separator 2-column variant (task-f0199aba)
A 29x2 input with full-width separator row 15 (both cells color 8) splits into two 14x2 fields: rows 1–14 use palette {7,9}, and rows 16–29 use {5,7}. Output is 14x2, omitting the separator. Compare aligned cells from the upper and lower fields: use the sole shared palette color (7 here) as the base, and put 3 wherever the aligned values are exactly equal. Test accepted with 0 wrong attempts after 3 prior incorrect submissions and an additional demo request. Accepted output:
`[[7,3],[3,7],[3,7],[7,3],[3,7],[7,3],[7,3],[3,3],[3,7],[3,3],[7,3],[7,3],[3,7],[7,7]]`.
This generalizes the confirmed vertical-separator equality rule to this horizontal-separator geometry: split into equal halves along the separator axis, compare corresponding field coordinates, mark equality with 3, and use the unique color in the intersection of the field palettes as the non-match base. For horizontal separators the output retains the original field width and has half the input row count; exclude the separator row. An earlier 2-column test with colors {8,1} above and {4,1} below had been unsuccessfully guessed; the confirmed rule indicates its likely output should be computed by same aligned equality and shared base 1, rather than marker/complement guesses. Keep distinction from the vertical case in implementation geometry, but the equality/base rule is shared.

- Additional accepted horizontal-separator instance (15x14): separator was row 8, all color 9. The upper 7x14 field had background 8 and sparse 1s; the lower 7x14 field had background 7 and sparse 1s. The two fields' only shared palette color was 1. None of the sparse 1s occupied the same aligned coordinate in both halves, so output was a uniform 7x14 grid of 1s. Accepted on first submission (0 wrong attempts). This directly confirms the horizontal split/equality rule for a wider field: remove separator, compare upper and lower cells by corresponding positions, initialize output with the unique shared palette color, and change to 3 only at exact equalities. For this instance no equal positions existed.

- Further accepted instance (task-f0199aba, 17x29): vertical separator column 15 (color 0) divides two 17x14 fields. Left field palette {2,9}; right field palette {5,9}; shared/base color is 9. Output is 17x14, with 3 exactly where aligned values across the separator are equal, otherwise 9. Accepted after one incorrect submission. The erroneous submission had a 3 at output row 3, column 9; the accepted output instead has it at row 3, column 10. Accepted 3 coordinates (1-based): (1,3), (2,11), (3,3), (3,10), (4,1), (6,6), (7,4), (9,2), (9,14), (10,11), (14,1). All other output cells are 9. This confirms that on these fields the right side's 9 cells match left-side background 9 at those aligned coordinates; do not shift positions or confuse local right-field columns with original grid columns (right local c = original c−15).

- Additional accepted vertical-separator instance (task-f0199aba, 12x15): separator column 8 (color 8) splits two 12x7 fields. Left palette {1,2}; right palette {1,4}; shared/base color is 1. Output is 12x7, with color 3 at exact coordinate-wise equalities and 1 elsewhere. Accepted 3 coordinates (1-based, field-relative): (1,4), (6,6), (11,3), (11,5). In particular, field-relative right column 4 means original input column 12; compare left c directly with right original c+8, and do not confuse input-column coordinates with output-local columns. The first output missed (1,4), while adding it made the output correct. This further confirms the shared-palette-base/equality rule for vertical separators.

## Additional accepted task-adfd3b86 instance: tiny 2-color checkerboard
Test input was `[[9,3],[0,9]]`; accepted output was `[[9,3],[3,9]]` with 0 wrong submissions after one demo request. The 0 at row 2, column 1 was replaced by 3 to complete the alternating checkerboard. For small grids, infer the periodic color pattern from the observed cells and replace inconsistent/background cells; here 9 occupies even 1-based row+column parity and 3 odd parity. This is consistent with the broader diagonal-periodic tiling family, but does not establish that all task instances are checkerboards—larger instances can encode longer cycles or horizontal stripe sequences, so inspect the input/demo structure.

## Horizontal stripe marker periodicity (task-adfd3b86; accepted)
Some task instances use entire horizontal rows as sparse samples of a 1D vertical color sequence, not a 2D diagonal tiling. Fill every row with the periodic sequence inferred from marked rows; replace background rows too. Accepted test: 25x25 input had full rows r5=3, r7=7, r18=9, r24=1 (1-based), all other rows 0. Correct output repeated the four-color sequence [3,9,7,1] down rows, with phase r1=3; equivalently output row color is [3,9,7,1][(r-1) mod 4]. Thus r5=3, r7=7, r18=9, r24=1 are consistent. Repeat each row color across all columns. This was accepted with no wrong submissions after 3 demos. Demo 1 confirms a related stripe case: output is an exactly repeated vertical sequence [9,2,1,4,8,5] across rows (period 6), extending colors through background rows. Do not infer row color by marker spacing alone where evidence identifies a short repeating cycle. Distinguish these horizontal-stripe instances from diagonal-marker tasks in the same family: inspect colored shape/orientation and demo outputs; diagonal motifs produce diagonal-shifted tilings, while full-width row markers can encode repeated row-color stripes.
